text:
A: Hello, Harriet, is it? Gareth.
B: Hi, yeah. Sorry, hi. Can you hear me?
A: Just about. You're nice and quiet, that's fine, I'll lean in. How've you found it so far?
B: Erm, better than I thought, actually. I was quite nervous before the first one.
A: You're doing grand. Last one for both of us, I think. I liked your bookcase in the photo, by the way. Proper reader's shelf, that, all stacked sideways.
B: [laughs] It's because there's no room. I work in a secondhand bookshop, so I keep bringing them home. What do you read?
A: Nature writing, mostly. Bit of local history. And a crime novel when I'm knackered. I've just finished one about the old packhorse routes over the Pennines, which sounds dull, but I loved it.
B: No, that sounds good. I'm doing history at Queen Mary, so local history's sort of my thing. East London, though. Women's lodging houses, Victorian.
A: Oh, that's interesting. Mill towns had a lot of that an' all. Young lasses coming in from the villages to work the looms and lodging with families. I think my great-gran was one.
B: Really? That's, sorry, that's actually really nice to hear. Usually when I say it people just go, oh, okay.
A: [laughs] Not from me. Where do you go to get out, then, in London? You look like you'd be a walker.
B: Erm, the Walthamstow Wetlands, mostly. It's reservoirs, so it's quite flat. There are loads of birds, but I don't actually know what any of them are.
A: Reservoirs, that's my world. I look after one in Darwen, I'm a countryside ranger. You'll have herons there, cormorants, maybe a little egret if you're lucky. Next time you're out, just listen for one bird and try and find it. That's how I started, as a lad.
B: Just one bird. Okay, I can do that. That's more manageable than my dissertation.
A: How's that going?
B: Honestly, badly. I'm about a third through. I've had an extension. I keep saying I'll make a plan and I haven't.
A: Well, I'll tell you a secret. I do my risk assessments the night before, every time. Twenty-two years and I've never learnt. You get there.
B: [laughs] That's reassuring, sort of.
A: Sort of. What's it like in Walthamstow, then? I've only been through on the train.
B: It's nice. We're above a nail bar, so it smells of acetone, but there's the market and the Turkish bakeries, and the William Morris Gallery's round the corner. I keep meaning to get a library card. And find a church, actually. I've been meaning to for a year.
A: Oh, are you church? I go to our parish one most months. I sing in a choir on a Tuesday as well, in the church hall. Honestly, I think it's the singing that does it for me more than the sermons.
B: Yeah. I think I miss the, I don't know, the people. Just having somewhere to go on a Sunday where nobody's asking about your deadlines.
A: Pick one with a decent choir and a cup of tea after. That's my advice. Nobody'll ask you about May, I promise.
B: [laughs] Okay. I might actually do that. I mean, I say that, but
